$comment: SPDX-License-Identifier: CC-BY-4.0 · The Kelvara basin, a hypothetical semi-arid river basin. Generated by packages/engine-py/analysis/kelvara_basin.py: every value is a typical literature value or a labelled convention, and derived values are computed there. Not a model of any real place.

sources.lenses: Blueprint v3.1 §6.1 example (enabled flags, plain names) and §1.4 (five classical lenses in v1.0)
sources.modules: Blueprint v3.1 §1.4 (Modules 2–5 in v1.1, Module 6 in v1.2)
sources.parameters: Model parameters not given here come from packages/scenarios/parameters.json (sourced registry)

name: Kelvara basin (hypothetical)

inflow.source: Hypothetical Kelvara River. Wet and dry cards read as the 80th and 20th percentiles of seasonal flow, CV ≈ 0.35, typical of semi-arid steppe rivers (McMahon et al. 1987: annual-flow CV ≈ 0.43 outside Australia and southern Africa). Deck 1 wet / 3 normal / 2 dry is a teaching convention.

reserve.source: About 12 % of mean flow: Tennant's 'minimum' (10 % of mean flow; Tennant 1976), below the 20–50 % of mean annual flow needed to keep a river in fair condition (Smakhtin et al. 2004). Stated openly in the game.

aquifer.source: Hypothetical shared alluvial aquifer of about 50 km² with specific yield about 0.10 (Johnson 1967), so 5 Mm³ of storage per metre of water-table change (ADR 0008). Full (20 Mm³) at 7 m depth; the low threshold, 15 Mm³, is 8 m, the suction limit of shallow pumps (Sekhri 2014); the reserve, 10 Mm³, is 9 m. Natural recharge 1 Mm³ per year ≈ 20 mm/yr, within the semi-arid range 0.2–35 mm/yr (Scanlon et al. 2006); a share of return flow recharges it too. One round is one irrigation year. Storage, depths and coupling are conventions.

orchardCrop.source: Orchard switches a scheme to the basin's orchard crop, the citrus of the Upper Citrus Estate, at the scheme's own area and irrigation method; values and sources as for scheme A

areaHa.source: a commercial estate; estates of 300–1,500 ha are common (Kan et al. 2024)

depthMm.source: citrus ET 900–1,200 mm/yr (Doorenbos & Kassam 1979 (FAO-33)); gross at drip efficiency

beta.source: drip field application efficiency 90 % (Brouwer, Prins & Heibloem 1989 (FAO training manual 4), Annex 1 Table 8); 88–90 % (Jägermeyr et al. 2015, HESS 19:3073, Table 5)

yieldTHa.source: citrus world average ≈ 16 t/ha (Steduto et al. 2012 (FAO-66), citrus chapter)

ky.source: midpoint of the citrus range 0.8–1.1 (Doorenbos & Kassam 1979 (FAO-33))

price.source: fruit (oranges, apples) FAOSTAT producer prices 2019–2023, median of six semi-arid countries, relative to wheat; real ratios vary 1–4× by country

kappa.source: capability conversion factor κ = 1 (no conversion handicap assumed)

people.source: (households + FTE hired workers) × 5: one owner household; hired orchard labour: 28.5 worker-days/ha/yr plus harvest scaled from 37.6 days at 35.9 t/ha to 16 t/ha (Junta de Andalucía, Costes de producción de la naranja 2022/23), in Eurostat annual work units. = (1 + 125.7) × 5, a typical estimate

areaHa.source: smallholder paddy; most farms are under 2 ha (Lowder et al. 2016)

depthMm.source: irrigated rice input 400 to > 2,000 mm, low end for low-percolation soils (Steduto et al. 2012 (FAO-66))

beta.source: surface (basin) application efficiency 60 % (Brouwer, Prins & Heibloem 1989 (FAO training manual 4), Annex 1 Table 8); 42–62 % (Jägermeyr et al. 2015, HESS 19:3073, Table 5)

yieldTHa.source: irrigated lowland rice in Asia averages about 5 t/ha (Steduto et al. 2012 (FAO-66))

ky.source: no FAO seasonal Ky for flooded rice; assumed between wheat (1.05–1.15) and maize (1.25)

price.source: paddy rice FAOSTAT producer prices 2019–2023, median of six semi-arid countries, relative to wheat; real ratios vary 1–4× by country

kappa.source: capability conversion factor κ = 1 (no conversion handicap assumed)

people.source: (households + FTE hired workers) × 5: about 1 ha per household; 84 % of the world's farms are under 2 ha (Lowder et al. 2016); hired rice labour about 290 h/ha/season (median of 19 Indian states, 2017-18 to 2021-22, DES Cost of Cultivation; family labour is counted through households), one season a year, in Eurostat annual work units. = (900 + 145.0) × 5, a typical estimate

areaHa.source: about 80 family farms of about 5 ha

depthMm.source: wheat ETm 450–650 mm (Doorenbos & Kassam 1979 (FAO-33)); gross at sprinkler efficiency

beta.source: sprinkler application efficiency 75 % (Brouwer, Prins & Heibloem 1989 (FAO training manual 4), Annex 1 Table 8); 69–78 % (Jägermeyr et al. 2015, HESS 19:3073, Table 5)

yieldTHa.source: irrigated wheat 4–10 t/ha (Steduto et al. 2012 (FAO-66)); good commercial 6–9 t/ha (Doorenbos & Kassam 1979 (FAO-33))

ky.source: winter wheat (Steduto et al. 2012 (FAO-66), Table 1, from Doorenbos & Kassam 1979 (FAO-33))

price.source: reference crop for the price ratios

kappa.source: capability conversion factor κ = 1 (no conversion handicap assumed)

people.source: (households + FTE hired workers) × 5: about 5 ha per family farm (assumed); hired wheat labour about 94 h/ha/season (median of 14 Indian states, DES Cost of Cultivation), in Eurostat annual work units. = (80 + 20.9) × 5, a typical estimate

pump.source: ADR 0008. capShare 0.5 inside the 0.38 (world) to 0.57 (South Asia) share of irrigation from groundwater (Siebert et al. 2010); cost is lift energy, linear in the head, costSlope = costBase × B₀ / (storage per metre × head at B₀) with head 7 m + 3 m; costBase is a convention in points.
